article.title: Regulatory Debate
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A gambling company used to be relatively easy to identify. It ran the betting shop, took the money and advertised under its own name. Online, that chain can involve half a dozen businesses before a customer ever reaches the actual operator. Someone might first read a review, follow an affiliate link, see an ad retargeted through social media and then use a payment service that has nothing to do with the site itself. None of those companies necessarily controls the product. They are still involved in getting it in front of people. Sweepstakes gaming has brought that awkward relationship into focus because regulators are no longer looking only at the company running the games. The category itself also takes some explaining. Many sweepstakes platforms use virtual currencies, sometimes with a second currency tied to prize redemption, and availability can change depending on the state. Reviews now spend a fair amount of time explaining those details, as Strafe highlights in their social gaming review series , where the differences between social play, sweepstakes coins and state restrictions are part of the discussion rather than something buried at the bottom of the page. That kind of information matters because the promotion of a product can travel much further than the product itself. The publisher is no longer standing outside the debate New York offers a good example of how wide the regulatory net can become . Its current law covering online sweepstakes games does not stop at operators. It also names payment processors, geolocation providers, platform providers, gaming-content suppliers and media affiliates among the businesses prohibited from supporting covered games in the state. For a media company, that changes the conversation considerably. A publisher can run an article about a service without operating that service, handling a customer's money or having any control over the game. If the article contains an affiliate arrangement, however, the relationship is no longer purely editorial either. This is not a new question. The Federal Trade Commission has long expected affiliate relationships to be disclosed clearly enough that readers understand when a publisher may earn money from a recommendation or link. What is newer is the possibility that a publisher also has to think about whether the underlying product can be promoted in every place where the article might be read. A website may have readers in all fifty states. The service being discussed may not. That mismatch is difficult to solve neatly. Search engines do not stop ranking an article at a state border, and an old review can continue attracting traffic long after the legal position around the product has changed. How far should responsibility travel? There is a reasonable argument behind broader regulation. If a product is restricted but the advertising network, payment system and affiliate traffic continue working exactly as before, the restriction has limited effect. The harder part is deciding how much responsibility belongs to each company in that chain. A payment processor can serve thousands of unrelated businesses. A publisher may cover several industries and have no role in the day-to-day operation of the companies it writes about. An ad platform can distribute campaigns automatically across a large network. They are all involved, but not in the same way. That distinction gets lost when every business surrounding a digital product is discussed as though it performs the same job. Publishers have their own decisions to make here. A review can be useful without being an endorsement, but the difference needs to be visible in the writing. If state availability is limited, saying so is more useful than pretending the internet has no geography. If an affiliate relationship exists, readers should not have to hunt for it. None of that settles the larger legal argument. It does make the media side of it easier to understand. The debate around sweepstakes gaming is likely to keep changing because the states are not all taking the same approach, and the companies involved are not limited to casino operators. What makes the subject interesting is that it exposes something much broader about online commerce: the company selling the product is now only one part of the route that brings people to it. Regulators are trying to work out how far along that route responsibility should extend. Publishers, advertisers and technology providers will have to work out where they stand before the answer becomes clearer.
